Tomato___Early_blight.description: Early blight is caused by the fungal pathogen Alternaria solani. It commonly produces target-like dark concentric rings on older leaves and stems.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings (target pattern) on lower leaves
Yellow halos around developing foliar lesions
Premature leaf drop and lower stem lesions
Reduced canopy and potential fruit sunscald
preventive_measures: Prune and safely discard affected lower leaves to halt spore spread.
Ensure adequate plant spacing (at least 45-60 cm) to encourage airflow.
Use drip irrigation or water at the base to keep foliage completely dry.
Rotate nightshade crops on a 2-3 year rotation cycle.
Apply clean straw or organic mulch around stems to prevent soil splash.
management: Remove and destroy severely blighted plant residue away from fields.
Apply protective copper-based or bio-fungicidal sprays during humid conditions.
Sterilize pruning shears and gardening tools between plants.
Ensure balanced soil nutrition; avoid excessive nitrogen that produces overly dense foliage.

Tomato___Late_blight.description: Late blight is a destructive disease caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans, capable of rapid spread during cool, wet, humid weather.
symptoms: Pale green, water-soaked lesions that rapidly enlarge and turn dark brown
White fungal-like cottony growth visible on the leaf undersides in humid conditions
Dark brown, greasy lesions appearing on petioles and stems
Firm, dark, sunken rot patches on green or ripening tomato fruits
preventive_measures: Use certified disease-free transplants and resistant tomato varieties.
Improve air circulation and avoid overhead sprinkler watering.
Space plants sufficiently and stake or trellis vines off the ground.
Eliminate volunteer tomato and potato plants from previous growing seasons.
management: Immediately rogue out and destroy severely infected plants to prevent field-wide epidemic.
Apply approved protective fungicide barriers before prolonged rain periods.
Refrain from working in fields when crops are wet to minimize mechanical transmission.
Dispose of infected plant matter by burying or sealing; avoid open compost piles.

Tomato___healthy.description: The tomato foliage exhibits vibrant green coloration, uniform leaf texture, and no detectable fungal, bacterial, or physiological damage.
symptoms: No visible spots, chlorosis, curling, or lesions observed on leaves
Firm stems and uniform green canopy vigor
preventive_measures: Maintain consistent, root-targeted irrigation schedules to prevent blossom end rot.
Continue regular inspections of lower leaf canopies once or twice weekly.
Provide sturdy stakes or trellises to keep foliage off the ground.
Maintain mulch layer to preserve moisture and suppress weeds.
management: Sustain balanced fertilization (NPK) according to soil test recommendations.
Keep field borders clean of weed hosts from the Solanaceae family.

Potato___Early_blight.description: Potato early blight, caused by Alternaria solani, impacts foliage and can diminish tuber size and yield under warm and humid microclimates.
symptoms: Small dark brown to black spots with concentric ring margins on mature leaves
Progressive yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding the spots
Leaf curling and premature defoliation starting from basal leaves
Dark, sunken circular lesions with raised margins on tubers
preventive_measures: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers in well-draining soils.
Practice 3-year crop rotations with non-solanaceous crops such as legumes or grains.
Maintain adequate plant spacing and uniform irrigation to avoid plant stress.
Avoid overhead irrigation in late afternoons.
management: Promptly remove and compost infected foliage hot or dispose off-site.
Apply preventive horticultural or copper sprays when weather indicates elevated blight risk.
Ensure optimal potassium and nitrogen balance to boost natural plant resilience.

Potato___Late_blight.description: Phytophthora infestans causes catastrophic foliar dieback and tuber rot in potatoes under cool, moisture-laden environmental conditions.
symptoms: Irregular water-soaked spots on leaves turning dark brown to purplish-black
Delicate white downy growth on the underside of leaves during high relative humidity
Blackened necrotic patches on stems leading to stem collapse
Granular brown dry rot spreading inwards beneath the skin of stored tubers
preventive_measures: Select certified blight-free certified seed tubers and resistant cultivars.
Hill soil well over tubers to prevent spore washdown during rain.
Destroy all cull piles and volunteer potato sprouts early in the season.
Monitor local agricultural blight forecast advisories.
management: Eradicate infected plants immediately upon early detection to protect surrounding crops.
Apply protective fungicides according to local agricultural extension warnings.
Kill potato vines at least 2 weeks before harvest to prevent tuber contamination at digging.

Potato___healthy.description: Potato foliage demonstrates healthy vegetative growth, robust chlorophyll synthesis, and absence of pathogenic foliar spotting.
symptoms: Vigorous green leaves with crisp margins and normal venation
Stems are firm and free of dark lesions or wilting signs
preventive_measures: Maintain steady hilling and moisture levels around root zones.
Scout fields periodically, especially after prolonged dew or rainfall.
Keep irrigation water away from direct foliar contact when feasible.
management: Continue standard soil nutrient management and seasonal weed cultivation.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: Bacterial spot on pepper is caused by Xanthomonas species. It thrives in warm, wet weather and spreads rapidly through splashing water and tools.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked, circular to irregular dark brown spots on leaves
Spots may have a yellow halo and centers may drop out creating a shot-hole appearance
Severe leaf yellowing and defoliation exposing peppers to sunscald
Raised, rough, scab-like spots on bell pepper fruit
preventive_measures: Use certified disease-free, hot-water treated seeds or resistant pepper hybrids.
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; employ drip tape or soaker hoses.
Never work with or harvest pepper plants when leaves are wet from rain or dew.
Sanitize stakes, containers, and tools regularly with disinfectant.
management: Remove and safely dispose of infected plants showing extensive bacterial spots.
Apply copper bactericide sprays combined with mancozeb as recommended by local extension.
Practice multi-year crop rotation avoiding other solanaceous crops.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: Bell pepper plant shows vibrant foliage, healthy dark green leaves, sturdy branching, and no symptoms of bacterial or viral infection.
symptoms: Uniform green leaves without spots, necrosis, or edge burning
Healthy branching stems and strong flowering/fruiting canopy
preventive_measures: Maintain steady root watering to avoid calcium deficiency and blossom end rot.
Provide supportive stakes or cages to keep heavy branches upright.
Mulch soil bed to stabilize moisture and reduce soil-borne pathogen splashing.
management: Monitor weekly for aphid or thrip vectors and inspect leaf undersides periodically.
